A graphical interpretation of the partial sums (Figure 10.13) shows how an alternating series converges to its limit L when the three conditions of Theorem 15 are satisfied with

N = 1. Starting from the origin of the x-axis, we lay off the positive distance s1 = u1. To find the point corresponding to s2 = u1 - u2, we back up a distance equal to u2. Since u2 … u1, we do not back up any farther than the origin. We continue in this seesaw fash- ion, backing up or going forward as the signs in the series demand. But for n Ú N, each forward or backward step is shorter than (or at most the same size as) the preceding step because un+1 … un. And since the nth term approaches zero as n increases, the size of step we take forward or backward gets smaller and smaller. We oscillate across the limit L, and the amplitude of oscillation approaches zero. The limit L lies between any two successive sums sn and sn+1 and hence differs from sn by an amount less than un+1.
